paras: The lynching of Dan Sale was the hanging of a Black man by a party of about twenty-five men near the village of Danburg, Wilkes County, Georgia, on the night of Sunday, May 6, 1888. Sale, accused of attempting to assault a white schoolteacher, Miss Sallie Smith, had been bound over by a justice of the peace when he was taken from a bailiff and hanged to a tree by the roadside. The story ran as a short Atlanta wire item from Washington to California, and a Savannah dispatch called it the only lynching ever to occur in Wilkes County.

Smith taught a school near the village, whose name the papers spelled as Danburg, Danburgh, Danbury and Danville. Most wire items named the accused man Dan Sale, while a later Atlanta report called him Daniel Sales and a dispatch from Union Point to the Savannah Morning News called him Daniel Hale. The Union Point dispatch said he "lived on the place," and the Atlanta report called him "a well known colored desperado."

According to the Union Point dispatch, on the night of Saturday, May 5, a man entered Smith's room, hid under the bed when she woke and screamed, and was recognized by her and her mother as he ran out. An Atlanta report printed by the Maysville Evening Bulletin on May 9 said instead that Smith was walking home from the schoolhouse on a woods road when she was seized and dragged toward a clump of woods, until her screams brought help. In that version, searchers found Sale near Petersburg toward morning and brought him back to the scene to be identified.

The Atlanta wire of May 7 said Sale "was caught attempting to commit an assault" on Smith, was taken before a justice of the peace, bound over, and put in charge of the bailiff. A party of twenty-five men then took him from the bailiff and hanged him to a tree by the roadside. The Savannah paper placed the lynching at midnight, while the Maysville account said a masked mob of about thirty men intercepted the officers taking him to the county jail and left him hanging until morning. Several reports said he had confessed or "acknowledged his guilt," but none named who heard the confession.

No report of an inquest, of arrests among the lynchers, or of grand jury action appears in the coverage. The only doubt raised in print came from the Fort Worth Daily Gazette, which reported that "some think hasty action was taken" because Sale was said to be of unsound mind. In late December 1888, two Michigan papers printed a year-end list headed "Victims of Judge Lynch" that entered, under May 6, "Dan Sale near Danburg, Ga."

Most papers carried the story as a brief Atlanta wire item dated May 7, printed on May 8 in the Omaha Daily Bee, the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, the Los Angeles Daily Herald, the Washington Critic, the Evening Star and the Fort Worth Daily Gazette. Headlines stated the accusation as fact: the Omaha Bee used "Lynched For Indecent Assault," the Maysville Evening Bulletin "Georgia Rapist Lynched," and Wisconsin's Wood County Reporter, on May 10, "A Colored Fiend Lynched." The Sacramento version said Sale had "confessed to outraging" Smith, and a one-line item in the Wyoming Tribune called him a "colored rapist," although most reports described an attempted assault.

The Savannah Morning News, the only Georgia paper in the coverage, headed its item "A Lynching in Wilkes" with the subhead "The Victim a Negro Who Entered a White Woman's Room at Night." The Fort Worth Daily Gazette alone framed the story around doubt, under the headline "Hasty Action" and the subhead "A Negro Lynched in Georgia Thought to Have Been of Unsound Mind," though its text repeated that he "acknowledged his guilt."

The accounts disagreed on the setting of the alleged attack, her bedroom at night in the Union Point dispatch and a woods road in the Atlanta report of May 9. They also differed on the mob's size, twenty-five or about thirty, and on whether Sale was in a bailiff's charge or being escorted to jail by officers.
